Reputable

/REP-yuh-tuh-bul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Reputable means having a good, trustworthy reputation; respectable and legitimate.

Reputable means having a good, trustworthy reputation; respectable and legitimate. Before hiring movers, Dad called three references to make sure the company was actually reputable.

Worked Example

Two listings offered the same guitar at the same price. The first seller had no reviews, a blurry photo, and wanted payment by gift card. The second had eight years on the platform, four hundred detailed reviews, a return policy, and answered Kira's questions within the hour. "Same guitar, but only one reputable seller," her brother said. "Pay the one with the track record."

The years of history, hundreds of reviews, clear policies, and prompt answers form the trustworthy track record that makes the second seller reputable — and the first one not.

How Reputable Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

Antonyms

shady

shady: of doubtful honesty

fly-by-night: unreliable and likely to vanish

How Strong Is It? — acceptable → distinguished → reputable

acceptable vs. reputable

acceptable vs. reputable: Acceptable means merely good enough; reputable means the good name has been checked and holds up — people vouch for it.

distinguished vs. reputable

distinguished vs. reputable: Distinguished goes beyond reputable: not just trustworthy, but standing out above its trustworthy peers.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again and again (Latin)

Root — put

Root — put: to think, to reckon (Latin putare)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: worthy of; able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Reputable builds on Latin putare, 'to think or reckon' — the root of compute (to reckon numbers) and dispute (to reckon against someone). With re-, 'again and again,' a reputation is literally what people keep reckoning about you over time, and reputable means that repeated public reckoning has come out in your favor.

Use the root in a new word: dispute

Use the root in a new word: dispute: In a dispute, two sides reckon the facts differently — the same Latin root putare, 'to think or reckon,' that decides whether a business is reckoned reputable.
